content: The majority of children experiencing their first episode of nephrotic syndrome achieve remission with corticosteroid therapy. However, some children either fail to respond to corticosteroids during their initial episode (referred to as initial resistance) or develop resistance after previously responding to corticosteroids (delayed resistance). For these cases, treatment options include immunosuppressive agents such as calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) like cyclosporin or tacrolimus, as well as non-immunosuppressive agents like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). Despite these treatments, the response rates remain limited, prompting the evaluation of newer therapeutic agents. This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks of various interventions for children with idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) who do not achieve remission after at least four weeks of daily corticosteroid therapy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs comparing different immunosuppressive or non-immunosuppressive agents with placebo, prednisone, or other treatments in children aged 3 months to 18 years. Studies involving both children and adults were included if pediatric data could be separated. A total of 25 studies involving 1,063 participants were included in the analysis. Fourteen studies had a low risk of bias for sequence generation and allocation concealment, while five and 19 studies had a low risk of performance and detection bias, respectively. Fourteen studies had a low risk of attrition bias, and 13 studies had a low risk of other biases. 1. Cyclosporin vs. Placebo/No Treatment: Cyclosporin may increase the likelihood of achieving complete remission (4 studies, 74 participants: risk ratio [RR] 3.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09 to 11.20) or complete/partial remission (4 studies, 74 participants: RR 3.15, 95% CI 1.04 to 9.57) within six months. However, the certainty of this evidence is low. It is unclear whether cyclosporin increases the risk of worsening hypertension or reduces the likelihood of progression to end-stage kidney disease due to very low certainty evidence. 2. Calcineurin Inhibitors (CNIs) vs. Intravenous Cyclophosphamide (IV CPA): CNIs may increase the likelihood of achieving complete or partial remission at 3 to 6 months (2 studies, 156 children: RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.25 to 3.13) and probably reduce the risk of treatment failure, including non-response, serious infections, or persistently elevated creatinine (1 study, 124 participants: RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.58). The risk of serious infections with CNIs appears to be similar to IV CPA (1 study, 131 participants: RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.56). 3. Tacrolimus vs. Cyclosporin: Tacrolimus may have little or no effect on the likelihood of achieving complete or partial remission (2 studies, 58 participants: RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.25) or on the risk of worsening hypertension (2 studies, 58 participants: RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.15). The certainty of this evidence is low. 4. Cyclosporin vs. Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF) and Dexamethasone: Cyclosporin probably has little or no effect on the likelihood of achieving complete or partial remission (1 study, 138 participants: RR 2.14, 95% CI 0.87 to 5.24) or on the risk of death or a 50% reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (1 study, 138 participants: RR 2.29, 95% CI 0.46 to 11.41). 5. Tacrolimus vs. MMF: Among children who achieved complete remission, tacrolimus may increase the likelihood of maintaining complete or partial remission for 12 months (1 study, 60 children: RR 2.01, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.07). The certainty of this evidence is low. 6. Oral Cyclophosphamide (CPA) with Prednisone vs. Prednisone Alone: Oral CPA combined with prednisone may have little or no effect on the likelihood of achieving complete remission (2 studies, 84 children: RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.87). Similarly, intravenous CPA compared with oral CPA (2 studies, 61 children: RR 1.58, 95% CI 0.65 to 3.85) or intravenous CPA plus dexamethasone (1 study, 49 children: RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.96) may have little or no effect on remission rates. 7. Rituximab and Cyclosporin vs. Cyclosporin Alone: It is uncertain whether the addition of rituximab to cyclosporin increases the likelihood of remission due to very low certainty evidence. 8. Adalimumab or Galactose vs. Conservative Therapy: The effects of adalimumab or galactose on remission rates are uncertain due to very low certainty evidence. 9. ACE Inhibitors and Proteinuria: Two studies suggested that ACE inhibitors may reduce proteinuria in children with SRNS. Additionally, one study reported that sparsentan, a dual angiotensin II and endothelin Type A receptor antagonist, may reduce proteinuria more effectively than the angiotensin receptor blocker irbesartan. In conclusion, current evidence suggests that CNIs may increase the likelihood of achieving complete or partial remission compared to placebo, no treatment, or cyclophosphamide. However, for other treatment regimens, the evidence remains uncertain due to low or very low certainty. Further well-designed, adequately powered RCTs are needed to evaluate alternative therapies for children with idiopathic SRNS. Future studies should focus on enrolling children from more clearly defined subgroups of SRNS to better understand treatment effects.
